St. Maria of Paris

Saints

St. Maria of Paris

St. Mother Maria Skobtsova · St. Elizaveta Pilenko

Period
1891–1945
Region
Riga;Anapa;Saint Petersburg;Paris;Ravensbrück
Titles / vocation
Martyr · Monastic · Woman · Writer
Commemoration
July 20

Introduction

St. Maria Skobtsova was a poet, emigrant, mother and Orthodox nun whose Paris hospitality became a refuge during the Nazi occupation. She was imprisoned and killed at Ravensbrück.

Read the published life [1]

Death / martyrdom

Killed in the Ravensbrück gas chamber;accounts differ about the final selection

Read circumstances and sources

Background

Born St. Elizaveta Pilenko in Riga, she grew up near the Black Sea. Her father’s death precipitated a period of atheism and involvement in literary and political circles. After revolution, two marriages and emigration, she arrived in Paris in 1923. The death of her daughter Anastasia intensified her work among people in need.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Childhood,emigration and bereavement

Life and notable events

Teva Regule’s 2018 sermon presents a recognizably complicated historical person: an educated intellectual, political activist, divorced woman and nun. It describes her Russian Student Christian Movement work and her Rue de Lourmel house as practical service rather than only discussion. She provided a fixed address needed for public assistance, cooked meals and offered counsel. During the occupation she helped Jewish people find safe places and assisted the resistance. The sermon locates her arrest within this wartime work and describes her continuing to share food and support fellow prisoners. Its interpretation is that of a named Orthodox preacher, distinct from the source’s biographical events.

[2] Published sermon,July15,2018 · Biographical middle and wartime service

She became a nun in 1932 with Metropolitan Evlogy’s support. Her houses served refugees, the homeless and the sick; she and Father Dimitri Klepinin later helped Jews obtain documents and escape routes.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Monastic profession and occupied Paris

Death and martyrdom

The OCA dates her death in the gas chamber to March 31, 1945. It explicitly reports conflicting accounts: whether she was selected or took another prisoner’s place. The substitution story is therefore not presented here as settled fact.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Final paragraphs

Writings and legacy

The Archdiocese’s 2026 commemoration identifies her as poet, artist, revolutionary, nun, resistance worker and martyr. It records recognition extending beyond Orthodox circles: the 1982 film, Yad Vashem’s 1985 Righteous Among the Nations distinction, a Catholic Worker house named for her, and a Paris street named in 2016. It also notes the preservation of her memory by the Protection parish and cooperation with the Compiègne deportation memorial. These are later commemorations, not additional episodes of her wartime life. The same ecclesiastical source identifies her 2004 canonization and remembers her death on March 31.

[3] Official commemorative news,March31,2026 · Commemorative article,recognition and parish memory

Regule dates the Ecumenical Patriarchate’s canonization act to January 16, 2004 and connects the commemoration with other martyrs of the Russian emigration in France. Her sermon is linked to the act rather than replacing it with an app-written account of ecclesiastical authority.

[2] Published sermon,July15,2018 · Closing canonization paragraph

The article also places her in the National Archives exhibition on women deported to Ravensbrück, held from February to June 2023. This contemporary museum context accompanies the Archdiocese’s account of continued parish remembrance and shows how her documented life is preserved through both church commemoration and the history of deportation.

[3] Official commemorative news,March31,2026 · National Archives exhibition and parish preservation
